title: 2 Samuel 23:18–39
context: The list continues with Abishai, who was chief of the three, and Benaiah, who did mighty deeds and was set over David’s guard, though neither attained to the Three. It then names the thirty, ending with Uriah the Hittite and a total of thirty-seven. Both traditions treat the list as shared ground honoring faithful service, and the names and numbers differ in places from 1 Chronicles 11, which are noted as textual issues.

verses.text: Abishai, the brother of Joab, the son of Zeruiah, was chief of the three. He lifted up his spear against three hundred and killed them, and had a name among the three.
verses.arminianNotes:
Abishai, brother of Joab, killed three hundred and “had a name among the three.” Arminian readers note that Abishai was a loyal and fierce supporter of David (cf. 1 Sam 26:6–9).

The relationship between “the three” and “the thirty” in these verses is debated.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see honor given to Abishai for his courage.

His earlier zeal to kill Saul was restrained by David (1 Sam 26:9), showing that courage needs godly direction.

verses.text: Wasn’t he most honorable of the three? Therefore he was made their captain. However he wasn’t included as one of the three.
verses.arminianNotes:
Abishai was most honorable of the three and their captain, “However he wasn’t included as one of the three.” Arminian readers note the puzzling wording, which interpreters discuss.

The text distinguishes leadership from membership in the elite group.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also note the difficulty of the verse.

The point is that Abishai held high honor without being counted among the Three.

verses.text: Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, the son of a valiant man of Kabzeel, who had done mighty deeds, killed the two sons of Ariel of Moab. He also went down and killed a lion in the middle of a pit in a time of snow.
verses.arminianNotes:
Benaiah son of Jehoiada killed the two sons of Ariel of Moab and a lion in a pit on a snowy day. Arminian readers note the vivid exploits that made him famous.

The meaning of “Ariel” is uncertain.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see God equipping Benaiah, who later served Solomon as commander of the army (1 Kings 2:35).

The deed in the pit “in a time of snow” is recorded as part of his reputation for courage.

verses.text: He killed a huge Egyptian, and the Egyptian had a spear in his hand; but he went down to him with a staff and plucked the spear out of the Egyptian’s hand, and killed him with his own spear.
verses.arminianNotes:
Benaiah killed a huge Egyptian with the Egyptian’s own spear. Arminian readers note the reversal: the stronger opponent falls by his own weapon.

1 Chronicles 11:23 gives the Egyptian’s height.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers recall David’s victory over Goliath with Goliath’s sword (1 Sam 17:51).

God gives victory to the seemingly weaker.

verses.text: Benaiah the son of Jehoiada did these things, and had a name among the three mighty men.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Benaiah the son of Jehoiada did these things, and had a name among the three mighty men.” Arminian readers note the summary of his honor.

The narrator again marks his reputation.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see honor given to faithful service, received as part of God’s provision of capable men for David’s kingdom.

Benaiah’s reputation rests on deeds rather than birth, which both traditions treat as shared ground.

verses.text: He was more honorable than the thirty, but he didn’t attain to the three. David set him over his guard.
verses.arminianNotes:
Benaiah was more honorable than the thirty but did not attain to the three; David set him over his guard. Arminian readers note that his trusted role shows David’s confidence in him.

Honor and responsibility are distinct.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the king placing a faithful man in a position of trust.

Benaiah’s later role under Solomon continues that trust (1 Kings 1:38).

verses.text: Asahel the brother of Joab was one of the thirty: Elhanan the son of Dodo of Bethlehem,
verses.arminianNotes:
Asahel, brother of Joab, heads the list of the thirty, followed by Elhanan son of Dodo of Bethlehem. Arminian readers note that Asahel had died earlier (2 Sam 2:23), so the list honors him posthumously.

The list includes men from many places.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see that faithful service is remembered even after death.

The list honors those who stood with David during his rise.

verses.text: Shammah the Harodite, Elika the Harodite,
verses.arminianNotes:
Shammah the Harodite and Elika the Harodite. Arminian readers note that two men share the same town designation.

1 Chronicles 11:27 gives a variant form of Shammah’s name.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see God’s people honored by name and hometown, an ordinary record of loyal service.

The spelling and town variants in 1 Chronicles 11:27 are noted as textual issues, not resolved.

verses.text: Helez the Paltite, Ira the son of Ikkesh the Tekoite,
verses.arminianNotes:
Helez the Paltite and Ira the son of Ikkesh the Tekoite. Arminian readers note the mention of Tekoa, later home of Amos (Amos 1:1).

Each name represents real service.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see individuals remembered by family and town, grounding the narrative in real people.

Both traditions treat these name lists as shared ground about God noticing faithful service.

verses.text: Abiezer the Anathothite, Mebunnai the Hushathite,
verses.arminianNotes:
Abiezer the Anathothite and Mebunnai the Hushathite. Arminian readers note that Anathoth was later Jeremiah’s hometown (Jer 1:1).

1 Chronicles 11:29 and 2 Samuel 21:18 have Sibbecai the Hushathite, a textual variant.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see faithfulness honored across Israel’s towns and clans.

The variant Mebunnai/Sibbecai is one of several in the list and is noted as a textual issue without resolution.

verses.text: Zalmon the Ahohite, Maharai the Netophathite,
verses.arminianNotes:
Zalmon the Ahohite and Maharai the Netophathite. Arminian readers note the variety of clans represented.

1 Chronicles 11:29 gives a different name in place of Zalmon.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the breadth of David’s support across Israel’s clans and towns.

1 Chronicles 11:29 has Ilai the Ahohite where this verse has Zalmon; the variant is noted without resolution.

verses.text: Heleb the son of Baanah the Netophathite, Ittai the son of Ribai of Gibeah of the children of Benjamin,
verses.arminianNotes:
Heleb son of Baanah the Netophathite and Ittai son of Ribai of Gibeah of Benjamin. Arminian readers note that a Benjamite, from Saul’s tribe, served David.

Loyalty crossed tribal lines.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see God drawing men from different tribes, including Saul’s own, to serve his chosen king.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: past loyalties did not bar faithful service under David.

verses.text: Benaiah a Pirathonite, Hiddai of the brooks of Gaash.
verses.arminianNotes:
Benaiah a Pirathonite and Hiddai of the brooks of Gaash. Arminian readers note that Gaash was near Joshua’s burial place (Josh 24:30).

The names continue.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see individuals from Ephraim’s hill country among David’s men.

The list honors many otherwise unknown men, a reminder shared by both traditions that God sees service history does not otherwise record.

verses.text: Abialbon the Arbathite, Azmaveth the Barhumite,
verses.arminianNotes:
Abialbon the Arbathite and Azmaveth the Barhumite. Arminian readers note that some of these places are uncertain.

The names are preserved as a record of service.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see faithful men remembered by name even where their towns cannot now be located with certainty.

Both traditions treat the list as shared ground on honoring service.

verses.text: Eliahba the Shaalbonite, the sons of Jashen, Jonathan,
verses.arminianNotes:
Eliahba the Shaalbonite, the sons of Jashen, Jonathan. Arminian readers note the textual difficulty of “the sons of Jashen.”

1 Chronicles 11:34 has a different form.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also note the difficulty of the Hebrew behind “the sons of Jashen, Jonathan.”

1 Chronicles 11:34 reads differently at this point; the variant is noted as a textual issue and left unresolved.

verses.text: Shammah the Hararite, Ahiam the son of Sharar the Ararite,
verses.arminianNotes:
Shammah the Hararite and Ahiam son of Sharar the Ararite. Arminian readers note that Shammah the Hararite also appears in verse 11.

Whether this is the same man is discussed.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the list continuing with men from different clans and places.

The repetition of the name Shammah the Hararite raises a textual question that is noted here without resolution.

verses.text: Eliphelet the son of Ahasbai, the son of the Maacathite, Eliam the son of Ahithophel the Gilonite,
verses.arminianNotes:
Eliphelet son of Ahasbai the Maacathite and Eliam son of Ahithophel the Gilonite. Arminian readers note Ahithophel, David’s counselor who later betrayed him (2 Sam 15:12).

Families could include both loyal and disloyal members.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the complexity of David’s court, where loyalty and betrayal could run through the same family.

1 Chronicles 11:35–36 has different names at this point; the variant is noted as a textual issue.

verses.text: Hezro the Carmelite, Paarai the Arbite,
verses.arminianNotes:
Hezro the Carmelite and Paarai the Arbite. Arminian readers note that Carmel was Nabal’s town (1 Sam 25:2).

The names continue.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see David’s supporters coming from many regions, including the area of his earlier wanderings.

The names differ in form in 1 Chronicles 11:37, a variant noted without resolution.

verses.text: Igal the son of Nathan of Zobah, Bani the Gadite,
verses.arminianNotes:
Igal son of Nathan of Zobah and Bani the Gadite. Arminian readers note that Zobah was an Aramean kingdom (2 Sam 8:3).

Foreigners served David.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see people from beyond Israel’s borders joining David’s service.

1 Chronicles 11:38 has “Joel the brother of Nathan” here instead of “Igal the son of Nathan”; the variant is noted as a textual issue.

verses.text: Zelek the Ammonite, Naharai the Beerothite, armor bearers to Joab the son of Zeruiah,
verses.arminianNotes:
Zelek the Ammonite and Naharai the Beerothite, armor bearers to Joab. Arminian readers note that an Ammonite is counted among David’s men.

Loyalty to David is not limited by nationality in this list.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise note that an Ammonite and a Beerothite served close to Joab as armor bearers.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the list records foreigners who joined Israel’s king in faithful service.

verses.text: Ira the Ithrite, Gareb the Ithrite,
verses.arminianNotes:
Ira the Ithrite and Gareb the Ithrite. Arminian readers note the clan of the Ithrites (1 Chron 2:53).

The list nears its end.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see faithful service recorded by clan and name as the list approaches its close.

Both traditions treat these short entries as shared ground, a record of real people who served David.

verses.text: and Uriah the Hittite: thirty-seven in all.
verses.arminianNotes:
“And Uriah the Hittite: thirty-seven in all.” Arminian readers note that the list ends soberly with Uriah, whom David wronged (2 Sam 11).

How the total of thirty-seven is reached is discussed by interpreters.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the narrator’s honesty in naming Uriah, a reminder of David’s sin.

1 Chronicles 11:41–47 continues with more names after Uriah.
